text: Hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you for joining me today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I hope everyone is having a great conference so far.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So my name is Dylan Cousin.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I am a Developer Relations Engineer at Quadrants.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the title of my talk today is The Frontier is Coming Home.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what do I mean by that?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And somewhere in the next few years, something smarter than all of us is going to exist.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've spent years asking when, but I think when is kind of the boring question.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think the real one is who it belongs to, because there are two versions of this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In one, superintelligence lives in someone else's data center, and you pay by the token.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the other, it's yours.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It learns from your life, your context stays private, and nobody can switch it off, throttle it, or take it away from you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That second version is what I want to talk about today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's the front you're coming home.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Quick thought experiments.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What would you build if your assistants actually remembered everything you ever taught it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every preference, every correction, every dead end for years.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's not a chatbot anymore.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's a second mind.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the assistant you're using right now forgets almost all of it the second the conversation ends.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every session starts from zero.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We call these things intelligence, and they are.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're just geniuses with no long-term memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This talk is about fixing that, not with a bigger prompt, with actual memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That genius used to only exist behind someone's API.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In a data center you'll never see, now it runs on hardware that most of us own.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not the absolute frontier, I'm going to be honest, but shockingly close.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A machine under $2,500 today can run what was basically last year's frontier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And OpenWeight's models are closing on fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The gap is shrinking every quarter.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You'd expect this to feel like a landmark, the frontier on your desk for the price of a laptop, and yet it doesn't quite land.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because a model on its own is just a brilliant stranger.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's powerful, but it isn't yours.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What makes it yours is everything it knows about you, and that part hasn't come home yet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can run a frontier class model on your own hardware today, and yet look at the AI stack that most of us are using today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The compute is rented.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The model is rented.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The harness is rented.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the part that's supposed to become you, the thing that should compound over the years, also rented.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If we don't fix that, the most powerful technology any of us will ever touch ends up owned by whoever holds the lease, not the people it was built for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's look at what renting actually costs today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Starts with where the model leads, because when you rent it, you don't really control it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This shows up in three different ways.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Last month, a government order pulled access to two flagship models, Fable and Mythos 5, for every single customer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now compare that to weights that are already sitting on your desk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Nobody can reach into your machine and flip those off.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even when the model stays up, it doesn't stay put.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Providers retire versions, and they throttle what's left when the economics get tight.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The model you rely on can quietly get worse or vanish.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Weights your own never change unless you change them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People also don't write prompts anymore.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're in agents or loops for hours.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And one task can burn thousands of times more tokens than a chat message.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some developers burn through over $5,000 a month of computes on a $200 plan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's a subsidy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And those subsidies will ultimately disappear.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you own the compute and the weights, the control comes back to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But that's still only half the problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's the deeper issue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Owning inference gives you autonomy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Nobody can take the model away.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But owning memory gives you continuity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And continuity is exactly what every major lab is trying to package up and sell back to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Look at last year.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every Frontier Lab shipped a memory feature, not because the models got smarter, but because they don't carry anything between sessions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That gap is the actual product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A system that starts simple and keeps learning you will always feel smarter than one that starts brilliant but forget everything about you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That compounding is where intelligence starts to feel personal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what actually is memory?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's not a bigger prompt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a system with three verbs, write, retrieve, and forget.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Same three things your brain actually does.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's an obvious pushback.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why not just throw everything in a big folder of marked-on files?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because retrieving the right memory beats dumping everything and praying the model finds it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Retrieval gives you something a prompt cannot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is control.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can filter by topic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can decay by recency and frequency.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can let relevance shift over time, the way human memory actually works.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the infrastructure has been ready for years.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: HNSW in 2016, embeddings have been running locally since 2019, long before any model could really use them at scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The memory side of superintelligence was never the hard part.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We were just pointing it at ourselves.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So today, the memory that actually knows you lands in one of two places.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Either it's stuck in an unindexed file you can't really query, or it's in someone else's cloud.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One terms of service change away from being reshaped or moved.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Carpathy framed it in a way that really stuck with me.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The model is the CPU, the context window is the RAM, and the memory is the disk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: RAM is fast, but forgets the moment the session ends.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The disk is what remembers you across every conversation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And right now, for almost every AI assistant on Earth, the disk is in someone else's data center.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So today I'm not going to argue which memory architecture wins or is the best one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's definitely a different talk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the disk, the parts that holds the actual record of you, should be yours fully and forever.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is the piece that I work on, and it's just one way to do it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I work on a vector search engine that embeds directly into your app.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It opens a local store inside your process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You write embeddings with payloads, then query offline in some millisecond time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Same REST core as Quadrant in the cloud, just running where you are.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With quantization, a million memories can fit in less than a gigabyte, small enough to live on a phone or even a Raspberry Pi.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Close the app, come back a year later, the memory is intact.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every app gets its own isolated store, and that folder is the thing that actually follows you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I'm going to do a quick live demo here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So right now, I have a video recording of a drone going over a house.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So basically, that drone, it's first time starting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's first time out in the world.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It doesn't know anything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this is actually running live right now, fully offline on my laptop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm using YOLO, which is an object detection model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it detects the objects and creates a label for every items it sees here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then we take that picture, we take that label, and we turn that into embeddings to create a live, real-time memory for that drone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that way the drone can remember everything it has ever seen before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so here you can see a 2D representation of the vector space with all the memories inside.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And memories that are the most similar will be the closest to each other.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So here you can see that we've already recognized 92 different objects and we have over 300 vectors.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's 300 different representations of those 90 objects.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can see that the entire memory and quadrants engine footprints is only 15 megabytes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then what we can do on those memory?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, we enable semantic search over those memories.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if I click here on the coffee table, you can see that in less than one millisecond I was able to pull up
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every single coffee table that this drone has seen before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we have the image here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have the first scene timestamp.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have the last scene timestamp.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a definition of that coffee table.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And also, we can see how many times that table has been seen.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is all being run and processed locally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's no network attachment at all.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we also have a capability of cloud sync.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for example, if you have a swarm of drones or robots navigating the world, they can have a hive mind in the cloud where one system learns something and they can all learn about it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And, you know, this was like an example for a drone, but you can apply that to everything, just a chatbot, an agent that you call to, a code assistant.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And, you know, if you create those memories for just a few weeks, the stranger just disappears.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It remembers your corrections, your preferences, the dead ends you had to only hit once.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A model that's merely good but never forgets you and keeps compounding over the years starts to feel superhuman in practice.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not because the model changed, but because it never stops learning you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's portable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Swap the reasoning model, change the hardware, none of it matters.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It all comes with you if you keep the same embedding model and that folder becomes permanent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lifetime of context, fully yours, moving from device to device.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we can go even further than that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, this can go way past a laptop or a drone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Point the same memory at your whole day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Where did I leave my badge?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What was her daughter's name again?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What was on that whiteboard?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what was the song that was playing when we met?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every one of those is just a retrieval query.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And, you know, you just watched a drawn remember object.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, extend that to everything you see and everything you hear.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And, you know, that's not science fiction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those are the smart glasses that are already shipping today and that we have seen today in this room.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's not a smarter you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a you that doesn't forget.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And right now, none of those devices share a memory that you actually own.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They could on your own terms.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because Frontier models are already building an index of you today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They have your relationships.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They have your habits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They have your whole inner life.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That index is common whether you opt in or not.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The only question is whether you own it or if you're renting access to yourself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And one last idea, because owning memory doesn't mean keeping it to yourself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Edge can seek parts of your store to the quadrant cloud out of the box when you choose to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Picture a family, each wearing glasses that record their own day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Separate memories, but they can pull into a hive mind the whole family owns.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Mom's day, Dad's day, your day, searchable together.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now scale that up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Instead of one company's super intelligence serving billions of identical people, you get thousands of small private ones, each shaped by a life, a family, a team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But that same mechanism cuts both ways.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A memory can be shared with Consent, or it can be extracted without it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's exactly why it has to start local and why sharing should always be opt-in, never the default.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You should really decide who gets your continuity and your memories.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is where I'm going to leave you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everyone here is going to watch super intelligence show up over the next few years.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That part is basically settled.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What's not settled is who it belongs to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's the fight worth having right now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: While the architecture is still up for grabs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So tonight, don't go home and just try a tool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Take the stranger home and give it memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then picture that memory five years from now, not a chatbot, a private mind that never forgets you, that nobody can switch off, and that knows you better than any system ever has, because you were the only one who ever trained it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's not a smaller superintelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's the only one worth wanting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All right.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's all for me.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you very much.
speaker: SPEAKER_00
